title: The pilgrim's beginning
hook: the Way of a Pilgrim: he hears pray without ceasing and sets off to learn how
tomorrow: what would a prayer sound like if it kept time with your heart?

segments.voice: Yesterday Deep River stood on this side of the Jordan, wanting home: deep river, my home. Today a different traveler sets out, and his road starts with one verse.

Phones ping all day: drink water, stand up, breathe. One line from Paul can't be set as a reminder at all: “Pray without ceasing.” A man in a Russian book, The Way of a Pilgrim, hears it read in church, and this time it stops him. People have to eat, work, sleep. How can anyone pray without ceasing? So he sets off with a knapsack, some dry bread and a Bible, to find out. Christians have answered his question in two different ways.
screen: `A LINE YOU CAN'T SCHEDULE.` → `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.` → `HE SETS OFF TO ASK.`

segments.voice: He asks preachers and learned people. They praise prayer, warmly. Nobody tells him how to do what Paul actually said. Here are the two answers his question runs between. The first is old. Origen, an early Christian teacher, wrote in his book On Prayer that whoever joins prayer to the deeds that are due, and right deeds to prayer, is praying without ceasing. The whole life becomes one great prayer. Meals, work, kindness, all of it counts. Its case: Paul can't mean words every second, so he must mean a life turned toward God. The second is the answer the pilgrim finally gets. An elder, a monk, listens to him and doesn't brush him off. Unceasing prayer, the elder says, is the Jesus Prayer: a short line said again and again, inwardly, from the heart. Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me. And he puts in the pilgrim's hands the Philokalia, an old collection of writings on prayer. Its case: a life only becomes prayer if something in it keeps praying. Both readings claim the same verse, and each has kept its own followers. What makes the pilgrim worth reading is that he won't take a fine answer that skips the hard word. Without ceasing. He wants the how, and he walks until he gets it.
screen: `NOBODY TELLS HIM HOW.` · `ONE: A WHOLE LIFE AS PRAYER.` · `TWO: A SHORT PRAYER, ALWAYS.` · `HE WON'T SKIP THE HARD WORD.` · then, large: `HOW TO PRAY ALWAYS?`

segments.voice: Choose one person whose way of praying, or of staying steady, you've wondered about: a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor. Write them a short message that asks it plainly, how do you pray? or what keeps you steady? Send it now or save it; for the rest of the sit, hold the question open, the way the pilgrim did.
The pilgrim's beginning. One line that won't let go, two old answers, and a man who walks until someone shows him how.
Carry this: how to pray always? He walked a long way rather than drop the hard word. That's sixteen sixty-nine.

screen: `DAY 1669 COUNTS.` → `SAINTS AND TEACHERS IN THEIR OWN WORDS · 68 OF 80.` → `TOMORROW: A PRAYER THAT KEEPS TIME WITH YOUR HEART?`

howItsDone: Some Orthodox Christians learn the Jesus Prayer from an elder or spiritual guide, as the pilgrim did, and some pray it with a prayer rope; other Christians speak of offering work and meals as part of a life of prayer.

chat.says: dad says he prays all shift at the firehouse, even on calls. that's just working, not praying. right?
options: Not so fast. One old reading says deeds joined to prayer make a whole life a prayer.
Right. Praying without ceasing means words only; work doesn't count at all.
Right. Nobody can pray on a call; Paul only meant pray very often.
chat.meaning: Origen read pray without ceasing as a whole life joined to prayer; the pilgrim's elder taught a short prayer kept going. Both are Christian readings.

Philokalia.meaning: an old collection of Orthodox writings on prayer

Jesus Prayer.meaning: the short prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me

Origen.meaning: an early Christian teacher who wrote a book On Prayer

elder.meaning: an experienced monk who guides others in prayer

The Way of a Pilgrim.meaning: a Russian book about a wanderer learning to pray always
